To reinvent something means to change it so deeply and completely that it becomes something essentially new — as if you threw away the old version and created it all over again from scratch.

The key word here is fundamentally. Reinventing something is not a small fix, not a simple update, not a surface-level makeover. It is a total overhaul — the kind of change where the final result barely resembles what it was before.

Think of it this way: if you polish a wooden chair, you've improved it. If you redesign it entirely — different materials, different shape, different purpose — you've reinvented it.
The Two Main Ways It's Used

1. Reinventing a thing, system, or organization

This is when something that already exists — a product, a company, a process, an art form — is transformed so radically that it becomes a whole new version of itself.

"Apple reinvented the phone when it launched the iPhone."

Before the iPhone, phones were devices you used to call people. After the iPhone, a phone became a pocket-sized computer that also made calls. The category of "phone" was reinvented.

"The streaming era reinvented how people watch television."

TV still exists, but its entire structure — how shows are made, released, and consumed — was rebuilt from the ground up.

Notice that in both cases, the name of the thing stayed the same (phone, television), but its nature changed profoundly.

2. Reinventing oneself

This is when a person deliberately and dramatically transforms their identity, image, career, or way of life. It suggests leaving behind who you were and constructing an almost entirely new version of yourself.

"After years as a lawyer, she reinvented herself as a painter."

"The pop star reinvented herself with every new album, adopting a completely different look and sound each time."

This usage is common in public life — celebrities, politicians, athletes, professionals — anyone who undergoes a significant personal transformation. It carries a sense of agency: the person chose to change, often because the old version wasn't working, or because they wanted growth.

This is one of the most common expressions using this word, and it carries a negative meaning — almost the opposite of the innovative sense above.

To reinvent the wheel means to waste time and effort creating something from scratch when a perfectly good version already exists.

"Don't reinvent the wheel — just use the library that's already been built for this."

A wheel is a simple, perfected invention. There is no reason to design a new one. So if someone "reinvents the wheel," they're doing unnecessary, redundant work. The phrase is a gentle criticism, suggesting someone is being inefficient by ignoring what's already available.

One of the most important things to understand about "reinvent" is that it implies wholesale transformation, not incremental improvement.

Compare these:

  • Update → small improvement, minor change
  • Reform → meaningful improvement within the existing structure
  • Redesign → significant changes to form or function
  • Reinvent → so radical a change that the old version is essentially gone

If a taxi company adds an app for booking rides, it has updated its service. But Uber didn't just update taxis — it tore apart the existing model and rebuilt the concept of urban transportation entirely. That is reinvention.
The Emotional and Cultural Weight of the Word

"Reinvent" is not a neutral, clinical word. It carries energy and ambition. When someone says they're going to reinvent something, there's an implicit boldness — a rejection of the status quo, a willingness to start over.

It's often used with admiration:

"She reinvented herself after failure and came back stronger than ever."

But it can also be used with skepticism:

"They keep saying they're going to reinvent healthcare, but nothing has actually changed."

To sharpen your understanding, here's what reinvent is not:

  • It is not simply fixing a problem. ("We fixed the bugs in the software" ≠ reinvention.)
  • It is not gradual evolution. Reinvention is deliberate and sudden by comparison.
  • It is not creating something for the very first time — that's just invent. Reinvention always assumes something already existed before the transformation.
  • It is not cosmetic change. Repainting a building is not reinventing it. Tearing it down and rebuilding it with a new purpose might be.
A Few More Sentences to Cement Your Understanding

"After losing its loyal customers, the brand had to reinvent itself to stay relevant."

"Some critics argue that modern art has reinvented what it means for something to be called 'beautiful.'"

"He reinvented his career at 50, leaving banking to become a wildlife photographer."

"There's no need to reinvent the wheel here — the solution already exists."

"The invention of the internet reinvented commerce, communication, and culture all at once."

To reinvent means to change something (or someone) so fundamentally and thoroughly that it essentially becomes new — either as a bold act of transformation or, in the phrase "reinvent the wheel," as a wasteful and unnecessary act of recreation.
